# Ekakanipāta (AN 1)

**ID:** AN 1  
**Section:** Aṅguttaranikāya (an)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Ekakanipāta

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Ekakanipāta* ("The Book of the Ones") constitutes the first major collection of the *Aṅguttaranikāya*, organizing teachings and doctrinal items into a single numerical classification [Bodhi 1970]. Across its various chapters, it presents short discourses centered on singular phenomena, ranging from the dangers of improper attention (*ayoniso manasikāra*) and unwholesome mental roots [Bodhi 1970] to the practice of mindfulness as a receptive middle path avoiding self-mortification and sense indulgence [Nauriyal 2006]. The nipāta famously includes passages affirming that the mind is fundamentally luminous (*pabhassara*) but corrupted by adventitious (*āgantuka*) defilements (AN 1.5–6, 1.10, and the "finger-snap" passages of AN 1.12ff), a doctrine that exerted long-standing influence across early Buddhist and later Mahāyāna thought [Almogi 2014; Nauriyal 2006; Powers 2016]. A major section is the *Etadaggavagga* (AN 1, chapter 14), in which the Buddha identifies eighty categories of foremost disciples, establishing the preeminence of figures such as Mahākassapa in ascetic (*dhuta*) practices, Anuruddha in concentration, Ānanda in personal attendance, and Bhaddā Kapilānī in the recollection of past lives [Nauriyal 2006; Nyanaponika, Hecker, and Bodhi 2003; Silk 1994]. In the commentary, the *Manorathapūraṇī* on the *Ekakanipāta* (*Ekakanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*) preserves influential accounts regarding the gradual decline and disappearance of the Buddha's dispensation (*sāsana*) [Turner 2009].

**Sources**

- [Bodhi 1970] Bhikkhu Bodhi, Anguttara Nikaya I (1970) — Structural definition of Ekakanipāta as single classifications, notes on AN 1:2.1–10, and doctrinal terms like improper attention.
- [Almogi 2014] Orna Almogi (ed.), Evolution of Scriptures, Formation of Canons: The Buddhist Case (2014) — Reference to AN 1.5–6 concerning the luminous mind defiled by adventitious blemishes.
- [Nauriyal 2006] D. K. Nauriyal (ed.), Buddhist Thought and Applied Psychological Research (2006) — Discussion of AN 1.10 on the luminous mind, AN 1.295 on mindfulness as a middle path, and AN 1.23 on Anuruddha's concentrative proficiency.
- [Powers 2016] John Powers (ed.), The Buddhist World (2016) — Reception of the 'finger snap' sutta on the mind (AN 1.12ff) in Mahāyāna thought.
- [Nyanaponika, Hecker, and Bodhi 2003] Nyanaponika Thera, Hellmuth Hecker, and Bhikkhu Bodhi, Great Disciples of the Buddha: Their Lives, Their Works, Their Legacy (2003) — Details of the Etadaggavagga (AN 1, chap. 14) listing eighty categories of foremost disciples, including Ānanda and Bhaddā Kapilānī.
- [Silk 1994] Jonathan A. Silk, The Origins and Early History of the Mahāratnakūṭa Tradition of Mahāyāna Buddhism (1994) — Citation of AN 1.23 designating Mahākassapa as foremost among dhuta practitioners.
- [Turner 2009] Alicia Marie Turner, Buddhism, Colonialism and the Boundaries of Religion: Theravada Buddhism in Burma, 1885–1920 (2009) — Account of the commentary Manorathapūraṇī on the Ekakanipāta regarding the decline and disappearance of the Sāsana.
